KEY MESSAGE 1... 

High pressure continues to move east of Nova Scotia this
morning with temps cooling into the 50s to lower 60s with some
patchy fog north/northeast of the Capital Region, where the 
skies are mainly clear with calm winds. A mid and upper level 
trough will move over the region today with some diurnally 
driven pop-up showers/thunderstorms over the southwest 
Adirondacks, eastern Catskills and the western Mohawk Valley. 
The mean MUCAPEs on the HREFs are 250-750 J/kg with very little 
deep shear of less than 15 KT. Pulse-type thunderstorms may 
occur with brief downpours. Severe weather is not expected due 
to limited instability and shear. Dewpoints will be in the 50s 
and enough subsidence from weak ridging downstream over the 
Canadian Maritimes will keep most of the region dry with 
humidity levels fairly comfortable. Max temps will be seasonable
with 80-85F readings in the valleys and mainly 70s over the 
hills and mtns. The isolated-widely scattered showers should 
diminish quickly with the loss of the diurnal heating. The skies
will become partly cloudy/mostly clear with light to calm winds
with some patchy fog developing north and west of Albany 
especially where any rain occurs. Lows will be milder in the 50s
to lower 60s. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

The weather pattern becomes very active Mon thru the mid week
with a potential late July moderate-heavy rain event/rainstorm 
Tue-Thu. Initially, a lead short-wave and a warm front 
associated with a low pressure system moving into the west- 
central Great Lakes Region will bring some scattered showers and
thunderstorms to the forecast area Mon-Mon night. The mid and 
upper level trough becomes more established over NY and New 
England. Clouds increase and dewpoints rise into the 60s. 
SBCAPEs increase into the 250-1000 J/kg range with very weak 
shear again less than 20 KT. Mid level lapse rates look weak. 
The shower/thunderstorm coverage will likely increase initially 
over and near the higher terrain and then spread eastward over 
the valleys slowly. The lack of shear will limit thunderstorms 
organization and limit any severe threat. We tried to keep PoPs 
in chance range 25-54% with some likely values over the 
southwest Dacks and eastern Catskills. General Thunder from SPC 
for Day 2 looks right based on the limited instability and weak 
shear. Max temps look similar to Sun with seasonable readings in
the mid 70s to mid 80s over the region. The shower and 
thunderstorms activity should diminish once again overnight with
milder temps in the mid 50s to mid 60s.

An impactful weather system looks to move into eastern NY and
western New England Tue into Thu. A strong short-wave trough
digs into the lower Great Lakes Region and Ohio Valley. Low and
mid level heights fall 2-3 STDEVs below normal. A primary low
pressure system moves over western NY and PA Tue pm with rain
beginning to over spreading the region with showers and some
thunderstorms. The EC continues to be further north holding the
primary Tue night into Wed with secondary low forming over
southeast PA and NJ. The GFS/CMC and several ensembles members
are further south and east with the secondary forming over
northern VA or the Delmarva Region which would bring moderate-
heavy rain into the region late Tue night thru Wed as the wave
moves northeast, and would perhaps limit the heavy rain to 
locations south and east of the Capital Region. PWATs do 
increase to 1.50" or so, and the NAEFS PWAT anomalies are +1-2 
STDEVs above normal. The 500 hPA low closes off over or near 
eastern NY and western New England, which slows the sfc cyclone
down which will be tapping Atlantic and Gulf moisture. The 
latest 01Z/26 NBM 48-hr probabilities > 1" of rain ending 
12Z/Thu are 65-85% across the region; >2" probabilities for the 
same time frame are 35-70% greatest south and east of the 
southern Dacks and the >3" probabilities are 30-50% from roughly
the Capital District south and east. A widespread 1.5-4" 
rainfall (some locally higher amounts over the eastern 
Catskills) over a 36-48 hr time frame are possible, but the QPF
continues to vary quite a bit with the guidance. 

Locations to the south and east of the Capital
District could receive the highest amounts and if confidence
increases later in time some locations could need a Flood Watch
due to training convection or slow moving rainbands causing poor
drainage and urban flooding or isolated to spotty scattered flash
flooding. WPC has issued a 'Slight Risk' for scattered 
instances of flash flooding from Albany south and east over the
eastern Catskills, mid Hudson Valley, southern Taconics, 
southern Berkshires and NW CT and a 'Marginal Risk' for isolated
instances for potential flash flooding in the newly updated Day
3 Excessive Rainfall Outlook /ERO/ for Tue-Tue night. The Day 4
ERO has the entire area in a 'Slight Risk' for Wed-Wed night, 
except for the southern Dacks, western Mohawk Valley and the 
Lake George Region. Dry anteceden
